content: The review on iron supplementation for reducing morbidity and mortality in children with HIV is outdated and has been replaced by a more recent review: Micronutrient supplementation for children with HIV infection by Irlam JH, Siegfried N, Visser ME, and Rollins NC, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2013 (Issue 10, Art. No.: CD010666). Anaemia is the most common haematologic abnormality in children with HIV, apart from CD4 lymphocytopenia. The mechanisms underlying HIV-associated anaemia are multifactorial. These include the direct suppressive effects of HIV on red blood cell precursors, the presence of other opportunistic or locally prevalent infections, deficiencies in micronutrients, anaemia of chronic disease, and the side effects of medications used to treat HIV or concurrent illnesses. Globally, iron deficiency is the leading cause of nutritional anaemia. There is significant geographical overlap between regions with high rates of iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) and paediatric HIV. Consequently, many children with HIV are also likely to be iron deficient. While the role of iron deficiency in contributing to anaemia in HIV-infected children has been described, it remains poorly understood. In many developing countries, where the burden of paediatric HIV is highest, iron supplementation is routinely administered to anaemic infants and children. However, this practice has not demonstrated clear benefits in most cases. Given the high prevalence of both iron deficiency and IDA in HIV-infected children in these regions, and concerns about potential adverse effects of iron supplementation, it is critical to evaluate the evidence supporting this intervention. The objective of this review was to determine whether iron supplementation improves clinical, immunologic, and virologic outcomes in children with HIV. To achieve this, a comprehensive search strategy was employed, developed by the Cochrane HIV/AIDS Review Group. The search included the following databases: MEDLINE (searched in November 2007), Embase (searched in December 2007), and CENTRAL (searched in December 2007). Additional searches were conducted in AIDSearch (December 2007) and NLM Gateway (December 2007) to identify relevant conference abstracts. Reference lists of eligible articles were also reviewed. The search was not restricted by language or publication status. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of iron supplementation in any form or dose, conducted in HIV-infected children aged 12 years or younger. The search results were independently screened to identify potentially relevant studies, and full articles were retrieved for further evaluation. The inclusion criteria were then independently applied to these studies. However, no RCTs meeting the selection criteria were identified. The main finding of this review is that no RCTs of iron supplementation in HIV-infected children were available. The authors concluded that the current clinical practice of iron supplementation in HIV-infected children is based on weak evidence, primarily derived from observational studies and expert opinions. For future research, the authors emphasized the urgent need for high-quality RCTs to evaluate the effects of iron supplementation in this population, particularly in regions with a high prevalence of HIV, iron deficiency anaemia, and malaria. They also recommended that policymakers prioritize funding for such trials to address this critical gap in evidence.
